title: Martinson & Berridge (2015) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False by checking each statement against its linked source segment. Distinguish empirical findings, cited critics' arguments, and the review authors' recommendations, while preserving the scope and strength of each claim.

items.prompt: Successful aging research expanded beyond Rowe and Kahn's endpoint criteria to include models describing processes that could lead to successful aging.
items.explanation: The introduction describes this expansion over the two decades preceding the review. Developing process models did not produce an agreed definition of successful aging.

items.prompt: Young and colleagues' graded approach allows for well-being, quality of life, and personal fulfillment through adaptation even in the presence of illness or disability.
items.explanation: Their approach includes physiological, psychological, and social dimensions. It defines successful aging in terms of using physical and social adaptive strategies to achieve well-being and fulfillment, including when illness or disability is present.
items.source: A graded approach to successful aging

items.prompt: In Hank's cross-national comparison, the U.S. successful aging rate of 11.9% ranked near the top of the countries compared.
items.explanation: Hank reported that the U.S. rate of 11.9% placed it in the middle of the comparison countries. This is a result from the cited study using particular criteria, not a current universal ranking.

items.prompt: The final set of 67 articles consisted only of empirical studies, with theoretical analyses and editorials excluded.
items.explanation: The 67 articles included empirical studies, theoretical analyses, and editorials selected because critiques of successful aging were central to them. The configurative review's four categories were distinguished by their recommendations for addressing problems, even when the criticisms overlapped.

items.prompt: The studies comparing objective criteria and self-assessments included findings that avoiding disability or chronic physical illness did not predict subjective successful aging.
items.explanation: The review reports this finding across three studies and notes that one also found functional status was not predictive. These results show that participants' evaluations need not match disease- and disability-avoidance criteria; they do not imply that health can never matter to those evaluations.

items.prompt: Critics of individualism argue that access to education, employment, housing, healthy food, and recreation can advantage privileged groups in meeting successful aging ideals.
items.explanation: These critics emphasize structural resources that favor privileged populations while marginalizing others. Their argument challenges explanations that place responsibility for meeting successful aging criteria entirely on individuals.

items.prompt: In the cited Japanese American study, independence meant prioritizing one's own needs over harmony with others.
items.explanation: Participants' accounts emphasized concern for others and adjusting personal needs to maintain group harmony. This is a finding from a particular study; the review also stresses diversity within cultures rather than one fixed meaning shared by every member.

items.prompt: The social justice critique calls for recognizing disability as part of human experience and acknowledging that all people are interdependent.
items.explanation: Stone argues that changing attitudes toward disability and recognizing interdependence are important for treating older adults as valued members of society. This is a normative argument for inclusion and dignity, not an experimental result.

items.prompt: Critics viewed the normative word successful as a value-neutral term that reduces comparison and hierarchy.
items.explanation: Holstein and Minkler argue that such terms are not neutral: they invite comparison, binary judgments, and hierarchical ranking. The critique concerns the moral judgments attached to the model's language.

items.prompt: The neoliberalism critique links emphasis on individual responsibility for physical and cognitive functioning to an expansion of the state's responsibility for social support.
items.explanation: The critics argue the opposite: emphasizing individual responsibility can support efforts to limit state responsibility for social support and for addressing structural inequities. This is the political interpretation advanced in the reviewed critiques.

items.prompt: The stated goals of antiaging practitioners in the cited research resembled the three components of Rowe and Kahn's successful aging model.
items.explanation: Flatt and colleagues reported this parallel, which the review discusses as a transfer of successful aging values into antiaging practice. It is not evidence that antiaging treatments are effective or an endorsement of those treatments.

items.prompt: The New Frames and Names alternatives retained disease- and disability-free aging as their core ideal and mainly changed the name or spiritual language of the model.
items.explanation: This group rejected foundational tenets of successful aging, including an unrealistic ideal of old age without illness or disability. Its alternatives incorporated loss, meaning, identity, and other dimensions, although many still focused on an individual ideal.

items.prompt: The authors suggest that successful versus unsuccessful aging and decline-oriented versus positive aging can be viewed as two forms of the same judgmental divide.
items.explanation: The discussion tentatively links the two binaries because both can rank ways of aging through value judgments. This is the authors' critical interpretation rather than a statistical equivalence between models.

items.prompt: The harmonious aging model criticized capitalist and consumerist ideals and emphasized human interdependence.
items.explanation: Liang and Luo criticized successful aging models for their capitalist and consumerist ideals and limited recognition of non-Western values. They proposed harmonious aging as an alternative centered on interdependence, challenges, and opportunities.

items.prompt: The authors conclude that repeated revisions resolved the conceptual confusion and recommend continued refinement of successful aging as the final task.
items.explanation: The authors argue that seeking one ideal model of individual aging is impossible and destructive because it devalues people outside its boundaries. They call for moving beyond successful aging toward conditions that allow people to thrive on their own terms.
